$comment: THE OWNER'S PALETTE, GIVEN AS A TABLE AND A :root BLOCK AND TAKEN AS GIVEN. What this register does with it is unchanged: every claim is RECOMPUTED by checks.py from the hexes in assets/css/europedoor.css, so a claim the arithmetic does not support fails the build. The instruction over the top of the colours is UI RESTRAINED, PHOTOGRAPHY RICH, MAPS PRECISE, TYPOGRAPHY DRAMATIC — an accent identifies a content family and is not sprayed across components, and the brighter colour comes from the photographs. The eight-hue OKLCH wheel this replaced satisfied every measurement here and was still the wrong answer, which is the difference between a palette and an instruction.
philosophy: European Future — editorial x architectural x cinematic x intelligent
gold: ADMITTED, AND THE RULE THAT REFUSED IT IS NARROWED RATHER THAN DELETED. European Future had no gold and two checks kept it out, because gold says luxury, premium, heritage, wealth and this product has to say Europe, discovery, movement, intelligence, culture, future. The owner's palette names ochre (#C49A52) as the TERRITORIAL accent for regions and events, which is a different job from a gold button: a ground and a kicker on two families, never the interactive colour and never the mark. So the refusal now names what it was protecting — no gold on an action, a link, a focus ring or the wordmark — and the two brasses it removed (#8a6d34, #c2a165) stay out by value.

discover.role: Light, warm, editorial, human. Where people fall in love with Europe: the homepage, destinations, places, experiences, culture, food, stories, photography-led browsing.

intelligence.role: Dark, graphite, quietly luminous. Where people meet the machine: the map, the planner, My Europe, search and filter intelligence, journey construction, personalisation, saved journeys, route intelligence, EuropeDoor Guide.

accents.$comment: THE COLOURS IDENTIFY A CONTENT FAMILY, AND NOT EVERY PAGE IS COLOURFUL — which is the owner's brief in its own words and the half that matters. An eight-hue wheel with a tinted ground per family was built, measured and removed: UI RESTRAINED, PHOTOGRAPHY RICH, MAPS PRECISE, TYPOGRAPHY DRAMATIC. So an accent is spent on the kicker, the section rule and the marks, the brighter colour comes from the photographs, and the primary action stays one interactive colour across the whole site — a button that changes hue by family is a family-coloured control, which is the thing the brief refuses. Five accents, each naming a family.

geographic.where: countries and journeys: where a thing IS, and movement between. Bone + cobalt + mineral

territorial.where: regions and the events calendar: an area and a season. Bone + ochre + mineral

architectural.where: destinations, stories and experiences — the human half. Bone + terracotta + photography

natural.where: provenance, heritage and the Fund: how this project knows what it claims

mediterranean.where: a GROUND and a mark, never text: the section rule under a journey or a region

machine.where: INTELLIGENCE only — /map, /plan, /my-europe, /search, /discover, which the brief names graphite + bone + cobalt and calls the instrument

cartography.$comment: TWO MAPS, AND THE SWAMP IS WHAT WENT. The objection to the previous instrument was not that it was dark, it was that it was GREEN: a near-black green ground under olive-green land reads as a marsh. The owner's correction is stated — no olive, the continent pale against graphite — and the light map is the European atlas.
cartography.why_a_separation_and_not_a_claim: A claim says a colour may carry TEXT; these say two drawn areas must be told apart. AND ON THE LIGHT MAP THEY CANNOT BE TOLD APART BY LUMINANCE AT ALL: land against water measures 1.18, so the BORDER carries the coastline and this register asserts the border rather than the fill. That is a printed atlas's answer and it is the first time this file has had to make it.

separations.why: SC 1.4.11 on the boundary of a graphical object — and on this map the boundary IS the map
the same edge read from the water side
a place name on the land it names
the continent pale against graphite, which is the whole of the dark map
the instrument's own accent on the instrument's own ground

ladder.$comment: The dark map is two values and a line; there is no ramp to order.

ratio.$comment: The ratio is the instruction, not the hex codes. A palette gives you a blue website with gold buttons; a ratio gives you European editorial design over futuristic infrastructure. It is measured on the pixels a reader is painted, over twelve pages spanning both worlds.
ratio.$measured: TO BE REMEASURED ON THIS PALETTE. The last reading on the previous one was bone 64.1, graphite 18.9, water 9.7, signature 7.0, accent 0.3 — and that 0.3 against a declared 5 is the finding this palette answers, by giving five families an accent that identifies them rather than two that tint a kicker.

$families.$comment: A HUE BAND CANNOT SEPARATE THE SIGNATURE FROM THE SEA ANY MORE, AND THAT IS ARITHMETIC RATHER THAN AN OPINION. The instrument classified every painted pixel by hue: water 170-218 degrees, signature 140-200, everything else the accent. The owner's palette puts pine at 174.2 and the map water at 174.5 — THREE TENTHS OF A DEGREE — so the water band swallowed the masthead and the run reported the signature at 0.1% against a declared 10. The bands were already data rather than a ternary, which is what let the failure be read at all, and data was not enough: two overlapping windows are two windows whichever file they live in. So a pixel is classified by the token it is NEAREST to, in OKLab, and the token says which family it belongs to. A lookup, never a shape — the sentence this repository already wrote about the credential scan and about the admitted golds. A pixel further than `max_distance` from every token is counted as neither: that is a photograph, a blend or a shadow, and calling it paper would be the instrument inventing a reading.

bone.role: the page. The owner's main background, and never #fff: white is a screen and bone is paper

bone-light.role: the LIFT above the page — a card, a field. The one surface that goes up rather than down

bone-2.role: the middle rung of the surface ladder, derived so bone -> bone-2 -> mineral is monotonic and every step is one a reader can see

mineral.role: warm stone: the third surface, and the land on the light map. One token for both, because they are the same material

ink-2.role: secondary type: a caption, a meta line, a subline

ink-3.role: the quietest type this palette allows on paper

rule.role: the hairline between two list rows, and nothing that is a boundary

ink.role: type. The owner's table names two near-blacks and this is the charcoal one; it was an alias for graphite, which made a page's letterforms and the instrument's field the same colour

pine.role: the masthead and the signature. A drawn colour before a read one

pine-deep.role: everything pine that is text, and the interactive colour on light

pine-air.role: the accent on the dark world's editorial surfaces

graphite.role: the near-black GREEN: a ground, and the instrument's field

graphite-3.role: the dark world's well — tracks, score bars, the deepest surface

cobalt.role: the geographic accent. Countries and journeys, and text at 5.68 on bone

cobalt-2.role: cobalt where it is pressed — the hover step under a cobalt link or kicker

cobalt-lift.role: cobalt where the ground is graphite, because cobalt itself is 2.98 there

cobalt-air.role: the instrument's accent on the instrument's own ground

sky.role: the Mediterranean and Alpine accent. A GROUND on light and a read colour on graphite

ochre.role: the territorial accent: regions and events. A ground and a mark, never an action

ochre-deep.role: ochre where it has to be read — a kicker on a region or a month

ochre-deep-2.role: ochre as emphasis rather than a ground: the year band’s current month, at 6.57 on bone

terracotta.role: the warm architectural accent: destinations and stories. A graphic at 3.58

terracotta-2.role: terracotta where it has to be read

terracotta-3.role: terracotta where it is pressed, at 6.35 on bone

terracotta-lift.role: the same accent on a dark ground

olive.role: the restrained natural accent: provenance, heritage, the fund

olive-2.role: olive where it has to be read on a lighter surface

warn.role: a travel advisory, and nothing else ever

warn-lift.role: the same warning on a dark ground

map-land.role: the light map's land. Mineral, because it is the same stone

map-water.role: the light map's water — and land against it is 1.18, which is why the border carries the coast

map-border.role: the coastline and the frontier on the light map. On this map the boundary IS the map

map-ink.role: a place name on the light map's land

map-dark-land.role: the continent, pale against graphite — the whole of the dark map

ocean-deep.role: a river on the land and the deepest sea: 3.90 on the stone, 4.62 on the water

ocean-mid.role: the step between, and the hero's own Atlantic

ocean-shallow.role: near water — the shore band under every coast

ocean-coastal.role: the shallowest step, where the sea meets the stone

forbidden.why: 3.58 — a graphic, not text. Use terracotta-2.
2.28 — a GROUND. Use ochre-deep where it has to be read.
2.12 — a ground on light; it is 7.96 on graphite, which is where it belongs.
2.98 — the geographic accent cannot be read on the instrument. Use cobalt-lift or cobalt-air.

never: gold or brass as a primary, a signature, or on anything interactive
navy and gold as the primary pair
generic tourism blue as a page background
gradient as decoration rather than as atmosphere
the letters A and I in the masthead, the navigation, or any h1
electric lime, anywhere: it was the dark world's accent and it ended up drawing continents

ultramarine as a CSS colour. It is real in this product and it is not a page colour: it is the violet end of the PLATE ramp, hue 244° in render.PLATE_HUES. As a custom property it was declared for the life of this palette and spent by no rule, while the register went on recomputing a contrast claim about it on every build — arithmetic about a colour the site does not ship

distinct.$comment: A CONTRAST RATIO CANNOT SAY THAT TWO COLOURS ARE DIFFERENT COLOURS. It is a ratio of luminances, so two hues at the same lightness always measure 1.0 — and every contrast check on this site passed while the advisory red and the cultural accent sat fourteen degrees apart at identical saturation and identical lightness. A travel advisory and a story kicker were the same colour to the eye, on the map, on the tags and in the notes. So a pair here must be told apart by HUE, which is the property a ratio cannot see — OR by luminance, which is the property a hue distance cannot see. EITHER, because the first version asked only for hue and the owner's own palette then refused it: ochre (hue 38, luminance 0.355) and terracotta (hue 16, 0.207) are 22 degrees apart against a floor of 25 and measure 1.57 against each other, which is not the same colour by any reading. The pair that created this block fails both tests — 14 degrees AND 1.22 — so the disjunction is still red on the thing it was written for, where a lowered hue floor would not have been.

surfaces.$comment: A SURFACE LADDER IS A LADDER, and a per-pair contrast claim cannot say so. The light world steps 1.09 and 1.12; the dark world stepped 1.12 and then 1.045, which is the card with a different name — so every track, well and score bar on a dark card was drawn on its own colour. Each consecutive pair has to be a step a reader can see.
